 📐 **Day 29-30 Development Log**

Date: 2026-03-08

Goal: Further code optimisations; caching & compute time

🔧 Technical Wins:
	• Implemented caching of reconstructed tectonic plate boundaries and coastlines, adding to the list of already-cached 
	  features: reconstructed land polygons, landmasks, reconstructed fossil locations. Caching precomputed features saves time.
	• Refactored feature & coastlines caching into separate functions; one for saving as cache, one for loading the cached file 
	  if it exists else reconstructing features, and a refactored reconstruct_to_lines function. 
	  This modularity avoids code repetition.
	• Runtime cut to ~7s for each frame.

To further cut runtime, I considered the following options:
	- caching the frame (i.e. At the UI step before plotting, so that plotting only renders an already-computed output).
				tectonics
				 ↓
				fossils
				 ↓
				UI
				 ↓
				plotting
	- a global cache encapsulating reconstructed tectonic plate boundaries and coastlines, reconstructed land polygons, landmasks, 
	  reconstructed fossil locations.
	- Turning plotting into a function of state rather than pointwise re-rendering.

None of these considerations led to direct code changes. But they were important exploration to know whether my existing architectural
approach was indeed the ideal way forward, or if there were more efficient ways.
In future, some of these changes may be implemented. But for now, the current approach is sufficient as my existing approach has 90%
of the yield of these approaches for no added complexity.

⚖️ Considerations:
  * #1 - Caching the frame
     	• An obvious speed upgrade. Then runtime would mostly come from rendering, not computation. 
	  However, notice:
		tectonics (parameter: tectonic_model)
		 ↓
		fossils   (parameters: species, number_of_specimens)
		 ↓
		UI        (parameter: time_slice)
		 ↓
		plotting

	  Meaning today I precompute all frames running from 0-70 Ma in steps of 5 Ma, for 4 T.rex...
	  What if a user tomorrow changes it to Triceratops?
	  All 15 frames will have to be computed again.
	  What if the species number changes to 73 Triceratops?
	  All combinations thereof will be cached, and take up scarce memory space on an 8 year-old laptop.
	
	  The bigger point is that state space rapidly explodes -
	  tectonics(models) x fossils(species, number) x time_slices

	  The goal is to save time, but complexity rapidly expands if every single frame combination is cached. 

  * #2 - Global master cache
     	• This would not even save time. This would mostly act as a consolidated cache manager.
	  But because of the same problem - state space rapidly explodes:
	  tectonics(models) x fossils(species, number) x time_slices
	  I would be caching an absurd amount of combinations. Again, added complexity for minimal gain.
	  Solving a problem no one asked me to solve.

  * #3 - Plotting as a function of state rather than pointwise re-rendering.

	Approach:
     	•  Define a class object 'Scene'
			class Scene:
			    def __init__(self):
			        self.fig = None
			        self.ax = None

			        self.landmask_img = None
			        self.boundary_lines = None
			        self.coastline_lines = None

			        self.fossil_artists = []

	   So that all key scientific outputs are stored as functions of state

     	•  Then build the functions create_scene() to initialise Scene, and update_scene to iteratively build out the other frames...
	   As opposed to the existing approach where every slider move recomputes tectonics, recomputes fossils, redraws landmask, recreates matplotlib artists.
	   
	   Plainly, instead of:
		render_landmask(ax, time)
		plot_reconstructed_features(...)
		plot_fossils(...)

	   We simply have:
		create once
		update thereafter

	   In theory, this sounded elegant. The plot_all() function was refactored into update_scene().
	   In practice, there was virtually no time saved. The time trackers from Day 28, I ported over.
	   Previously, the bottleneck in my plot_all() approach was plotting the plate features.
	   This time, the bottleneck was landmask rendering.
	   The idea was the landmask should update on itself, i.e.
		scene.landmask_img = render_landmask(ax, time, RES_DEG, img=scene.landmask_img)
	   However in practice this caused the continents to "spill out" of their boundaries. A projection issue.
	   The way I tried to solve it was with
		scene.landmask_img.remove()
		scene.landmask_img = render_landmask(ax, time, RES_DEG, img=scene.landmask_img)
	   But that meant deleting the landmask every time and re-rendering it, defeating the whole purpose of updating as a function of state.
	   And in terms of concrete outcomes, it pushed the rendering time right up from 0.04s to 4.5s because of the re-projection,
	   which was exactly the computational bottleneck in my earlier plot_all() approach.
	   Overall, there was no change to overall compute time ~7-9s and it may have in fact been slower.
	   I ditched this approach.

💡 Insights: 
 - Caching sounds great, but what are you caching? You can save on rendering time, but if the state space explodes, you raise the memory storage.
 - A different approach may sound great but if it does not buy you concrete wins, is it worth doing?
 - Sometimes "optimisation" incurs tradeoffs (time vs memory). 
 - Question: what are you optimising toward? What is your objective function?
 - Caching at the layer level, rather than caching at the output level, was the correct layer of abstraction for an engine that aims to support 
   20++ different species, >1000 specimens each; especially one designed for interactivity where the selectin criteria are always changing.

				"trex":68,
				"triceratops":70,
				"velociraptor":75
}
• Build a Panel grid
• Connect each image to render_time
• Build an interactive_renderer.py module for hover-click-pop-ups. The current matplotlib renderer that lives in ui.py is insufficient.

For optimisation - 
• Cache reconstructed fossil locations for faster compute time. 
  Landmask (for raster colouring), continental_polygons (also raster) & theropods.csv (raw input data from PBDB) 
  have all been cached, but I notice that the fossil locations are being reconstructed every time,
  when it would be more efficient to reconstruct them once, then cache the results and reuse them subsequently.
• Trim whitespace in exported .png images.
• Investigate why exported .mp4 deep-time playbacks have the first 3-5s blank.
